scenario_prompt: Write the response to this scored RFP question, worth 25% of the RFP's overall technical score: "Describe the migration approach and cutover plan." Context: the migration moves load-matching and carrier-settlement systems off on-premises Microsoft SQL Server (28 instances, 620 Hyper-V virtual machines) onto Google Cloud (Google Compute Engine for compute, Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL for the data layer), within a 2-year, $4,200,000 programme, with proposals due 2026-11-15 and the buyer's next compliance audit opening in 6 months. Return only the answer text, no section headers beyond what the answer itself needs.
text:
Before drafting, a quick note: I'm treating the RFP question text and the facts given in your message (instance/VM counts, target stack, budget, timeline, audit date) as the only customer source material supplied for this task. No discovery notes, incumbent architecture diagrams, or stated SLAs/RTOs were provided, so I can't invoke the customer's-own-term retention rule beyond that text, and several figures below are marked as gaps rather than invented.

**RFP answer**

Today, load-matching and carrier-settlement run on 28 Microsoft SQL Server instances across 620 Hyper-V virtual machines, entirely on-premises. That footprint carries fixed hardware refresh and Hyper-V licensing cost, and it sits inside a compliance regime whose next audit opens in six months — before a full re-platform could plausibly finish. The migration moves this estate to Google Compute Engine for compute and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL for the data layer, inside a 2-year, $4,200,000 programme, without breaking that audit's evidence trail.

**Approach: assess, foundation, wave, verify, cut over**

We start with a discovery and dependency-mapping phase across all 28 SQL Server instances, because load-matching and settlement share reference data and job schedules that determine safe migration order. [PF-2.4 GAP: current inter-instance dependency map and data volumes were not supplied — needed to sequence waves and size Cloud SQL instances.] Landing-zone work follows: GCE project structure, VPC design, IAM, and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instances sized to replace the Hyper-V-hosted SQL Server tier.

You then move workloads in waves, not as one cutover. Each wave covers one bounded set of instances — for example settlement reporting before settlement transaction processing — so a failed wave never blocks the whole programme. Schema and data conversion from SQL Server T-SQL to PostgreSQL runs through an assessment-and-conversion tool followed by manual remediation of incompatible objects (stored procedures, triggers, proprietary functions), since SQL Server and PostgreSQL are not wire-compatible. [PF-2.4 GAP: the proportion of T-SQL-specific logic (stored procedures, CLR objects) in the current estate was not supplied — this drives conversion effort and wave duration estimates.] Continuous replication (CDC) keeps each converted PostgreSQL instance in sync with its SQL Server source during the wave, so cutover for that wave is a switch of write traffic, not a bulk data copy.

**Cutover plan**

Each wave's cutover follows the same sequence: freeze non-essential writes to the source instance, let CDC drain the remaining change backlog, run data-parity checks between source and target, redirect application connection strings to Cloud SQL, then unfreeze writes. [PF-2.4 GAP: no maximum acceptable write-freeze window was supplied — this is normally set by the business owner of load-matching, since a freeze during active load-matching directly affects carrier throughput.] A rollback plan for each wave keeps the SQL Server source live and receiving read-only replication for a defined window after cutover, so traffic can revert to it if parity checks or post-cutover monitoring surface an issue.

Given the compliance audit opens in six months, the first waves target instances outside the audit's scope, and any instance still mid-migration when the audit opens keeps its SQL Server source as system of record with Cloud SQL running read-only, so the audit trail is never split across two authoritative systems. [PF-2.4 GAP: which of the 28 instances fall inside the upcoming audit's scope was not supplied — this determines the wave order and is a decision for you, the compliance owner, to confirm before wave sequencing is finalized.] [PF-2.14 REVIEW (commitment): the statement that audited instances stay unmigrated until after the audit closes is a scheduling commitment and should be confirmed against your actual audit scope before this proposal is finalized.]

**Metrics and proof**

Programme duration and wave count size to the 2-year, $4,200,000 budget, sequencing the highest-risk, highest-dependency instances (settlement) after load-matching instances, where CDC and parity-check tooling can be proven at lower risk first. [PF-1.13/PF-1.14 — no current downtime, RTO/RPO, or throughput baseline for load-matching or settlement was supplied; without it we cannot state a numeric improvement target.] [PF-2.4 GAP: baseline figures for current MTTR, transaction volume, or settlement processing time — needed to define migration success metrics and to size Cloud SQL instances correctly.]

## Unresolved before this document is sent

| Marker | Rule | What is needed |
|---|---|---|
| Inter-instance dependency map and data volumes not supplied | PF-2.4 | Current dependency map and data volumes across the 28 instances, to sequence waves and size Cloud SQL |
| T-SQL-specific logic proportion not supplied | PF-2.4 | Estimate of stored-procedure/CLR/proprietary-object volume, to size conversion effort |
| Maximum acceptable write-freeze window not supplied | PF-2.4 | Business-owner-defined cutover freeze tolerance for load-matching and settlement |
| Audit scope across the 28 instances not supplied | PF-2.4 | Which instances fall inside the upcoming compliance audit, to finalize wave order |
| Commitment to hold audited instances unmigrated until after audit closes | PF-2.14 REVIEW (commitment) | Confirmation this scheduling commitment matches actual audit scope and buyer expectations |
| No downtime/RTO/RPO/throughput baseline supplied | PF-2.4 | Current baseline figures for MTTR, transaction volume, settlement processing time |
